statement: Human cerebral cortex is 1 to 4.5 mm thick with an overall average of about 2.5 mm (MRI). In human temporal cortex layer 4 ends about 1.6 mm below the pia and the grey/white border lies at about 2.8 mm; layer 5 begins about 1.5 mm below the pia, and patch-clamped human layer-5 pyramidal cell bodies lay 1.46 to 2.15 mm below the pial surface (means about 1.8 mm). The drawings place the cell body 1.6 mm below the surface.
sources: Fischl B, Dale AM (2000). Measuring the thickness of the human cerebral cortex from magnetic resonance images. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA 97(20):11050–11055 doi:10.1073/pnas.200033797

statement: During relaxed wakefulness the EEG shows alpha (8–13 Hz) activity on which the thalamus is a strong influence; two thalamic cellular mechanisms, high-threshold burst firing in a subset of thalamocortical neurons and the interconnection of that subset by gap junctions, combine to generate locally synchronised alpha activity, and the same machinery yields theta (2–7 Hz) when the thalamocortical neurons are less depolarised.
sources: Hughes SW, Crunelli V (2005). Thalamic mechanisms of EEG alpha rhythms and their pathological implications. The Neuroscientist 11(4):357–372 doi:10.1177/1073858405277450

statement: Gamma oscillations (30–90 Hz) are generated by networks of inhibitory interneurons acting through GABA-A synapses; perisomatic inhibition by fast-spiking basket cells is the key synchronising ingredient, a network of mutually connected interneurons needs only mutual inhibition, the GABA-A time constant and enough drive to oscillate at gamma, and perisomatic inhibitory potentials synchronise neurons far more effectively than dendritic excitatory ones.
sources: Buzsáki G, Wang X-J (2012). Mechanisms of gamma oscillations. Annual Review of Neuroscience 35:203–225 doi:10.1146/annurev-neuro-062111-150444

statement: Cortical activity also propagates as travelling waves at two scales carried by distinct axon populations: mesoscopic waves within one cortical area at speeds consistent with unmyelinated layer 2/3 horizontal fibres (0.1–0.8 m/s), and macroscopic waves spanning centimetres at 1–10 m/s, within the range of myelinated white-matter conduction; human ECoG sleep-spindle and alpha waves cluster at 2–5 m/s.
sources: Muller L, Chavane F, Reynolds J, Sejnowski TJ (2018). Cortical travelling waves: mechanisms and computational principles. Nature Reviews Neuroscience 19(5):255–268 doi:10.1038/nrn.2018.20

statement: A systematic review of low-cost consumer EEG headsets states that most use dry electrodes, naming the InteraXon Muse (dry electrodes at FPz, AF7, AF8, TP9 and TP10) and the single-channel NeuroSky MindWave (dry forehead electrode with an ear-clip reference); the Dreem sleep headband uses five dry silicone electrodes with protrusions that reach the scalp through hair, and Bitbrain’s Diadem uses 12 dry sensors with no gel; by contrast the Emotiv EPOC X uses saline-based sensors and the Emotiv Insight semi-dry polymer sensors.
sources: LaRocco J, Le MD, Paeng D-G (2020). A systemic review of available low-cost EEG headsets used for drowsiness detection. Frontiers in Neuroinformatics 14:553352 doi:10.3389/fninf.2020.553352

statement: Modelling choice: 10 µV rms of muscle noise in the 20–300 Hz band for a relaxed subject at a mid-scalp site, with 100 µV as the clenched-jaw value at a temporal site. Measured support: muscle activity at temporal EEG electrodes can reach about 100 µV against neural gamma below 1 µV; even at central electrodes in resting subjects, scalp EEG above 20 Hz is mostly muscle, with about 5 times more power at 40 Hz and 10 times at 80 Hz than under paralysis (10- to 200-fold differences above 20 Hz); on skin away from cranial muscles, resting muscle adds negligibly to electrode noise.
sources: Muthukumaraswamy SD (2013). High-frequency brain activity and muscle artifacts in MEG/EEG: a review and recommendations. Frontiers in Human Neuroscience 7:138 doi:10.3389/fnhum.2013.00138

statement: The 20 µV alpha rhythm used in sections 4 and 5 is not an independent choice: in the section 3 head (radial source 2 mm below the cortical surface, default layer thicknesses and conductivities) the scalp potential is 0.54 µV per nA·m, so 20 µV corresponds to an equivalent dipole of about 37 nA·m, which at 0.5 pA·m per cell is about 7 × 10⁴ perfectly synchronous pyramidal cells (more with partial synchrony), within the tens-of-thousands range quoted for a typical source.
sources: Malmivuo J, Plonsey R (1995). Bioelectromagnetism: Principles and Applications of Bioelectric and Biomagnetic Fields. Oxford University Press Ch. 7 (quasistatic conditions), Ch. 8 (source–field models, eqs 8.7 and 8.15), Ch. 13 (EEG) https://www.bem.fi/book/
